title: Preface — How People Know Their Country
paragraphs: Basso begins with a question he says is as old as people and places themselves: what do people make of places? It sounds simple, and that is exactly the trouble. Our attachments to place are so easily sustained that we take them for granted, like a fondness for certain colours or foods — until we are deprived of them and find ourselves adrift, dislocated in surroundings we neither understand nor care for. Then a sense of place asserts itself in powerful ways, and its subtler components (absent smells in the air, not enough visible sky) come surging into awareness. Places, he concludes, are as much a part of us as we are of them.

He first went to Cibecue, on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation in Arizona, in the summer of 1959, as a nineteen-year-old college student. Decades later he was still going, and the essays gathered here come out of a long-range project in Western Apache cultural geography: to record on topographic maps the approximate location of every Apache-named place within twenty miles of the community. Residents had never had maps they considered their own — the existing ones showed a handful of places under extraneous English and Spanish names — and the work was intended to lay the foundation for a local Apache atlas. Some in Cibecue thought it long overdue.

The phrase that names the subject comes from Ronnie Lupe, then chairman of the White Mountain Apache Tribe: how people know their country. Basso's own gloss is a complaint about his discipline. Places are constantly mentioned in ethnographic writing — the people of X, the hamlet of Y, the marketplace at Z — but almost always in passing, early on, and chiefly to locate the text itself. Then the text moves on without a backward glance. Cultural anthropologists have worked for years in communities where ties to place are deep and vital, and have had remarkably little to say about them.

So the four chapters are four approaches to one topic, each centred on a different Apache person: not only because each figured centrally in the work, but because senses of place, however much they draw on shared local knowledge, are finally the possessions of particular individuals. Basso is firm about this qualification, and it matters for reading the whole book: people, not cultures, sense places — and in Cibecue, as anywhere, they do so in varying ways.

He is also candid about what he owes. His debt to the Apache people of Cibecue reaches back more than thirty-five years, and he names the horsemen — Morley Cromwell, Charles Henry, Robert Machuse, Nick Thompson, Dudley Patterson — as the best teachers and finest friends anyone could ask for. All of them, he writes, are with the ancestors now, and he hears their voices as he travels through their country. They were pleased that some of their knowledge would be preserved and made public, subject to clearly defined restrictions which he says have not been and never shall be violated. The book is theirs, a gift to the grandchildren of Cibecue.
